blocks.content: The previous topic established why organizations adopt cloud computing. This topic answers the next natural question: adopt it how? Not every organization implements cloud computing the exact same way, and the differences matter.
1. Cloud Deployment Models, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: 1. Cloud Deployment Models, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: A cloud deployment model describes exactly where an organization's computing infrastructure physically lives, who owns it, and who else, if anyone, shares access to that same underlying infrastructure alongside that organization.

This is a genuinely distinct question from the service model question, IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS, covered in a later topic in this module. Deployment model is about where and with whom, service model is about how much of the stack you manage yourself.

Three deployment models cover the overwhelming majority of real world arrangements: public cloud, private cloud, and hybrid cloud, each representing a different answer to the where and with whom question.
This topic introduces all three at a high level, with the very next topic giving each one its own full, dedicated, side by side comparison and depth.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736020856-384583286.png
blocks.alt: Cloud deployment models given its own full depth

blocks.content: 2. Where Infrastructure Actually Lives

In public cloud, infrastructure lives in a provider's own data centers, such as AWS's global infrastructure covered later in this module, shared across many customers through the resource pooling characteristic established in the first topic of this module.

In private cloud, infrastructure is dedicated entirely to one organization, either physically on premises in that organization's own facility or hosted by a third party but never shared with any other customer.

In hybrid cloud, infrastructure spans both arrangements simultaneously, with some workloads running in public cloud and others running in private infrastructure, connected together and often moving between the two as needs change.

Determining which of these three arrangements fits a given organization, or a given specific workload within that organization, is a genuine architectural decision with real, lasting consequences for cost, control, and operational responsibility.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736023540-172690337.png
blocks.alt: An answer to exactly where an organization's infrastructure actually lives

blocks.content: 3. A Real Deployment Models Example

Consider a bank that must comply with strict regulatory requirements around where certain categories of customer financial data can physically reside, while also wanting to run a modern, fast moving public facing website.

The bank's core banking systems, handling sensitive regulated data, run on private cloud infrastructure, giving the bank full, exclusive control over exactly where that data lives and exactly who can access the underlying hardware.

The bank's public website and marketing pages, with no such regulatory sensitivity, run entirely on AWS public cloud, benefiting fully from the elasticity, global reach, and reduced operational burden covered in the previous topic.

This combination, different deployment models for different workloads within the exact same organization, is a hybrid cloud arrangement, and it is a genuinely common pattern for organizations with a mix of regulated and unregulated workloads.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736025217-754356928.png
blocks.alt: A bank running core banking on private and web on public cloud

blocks.content: 4. Recap: The Why This Topic Puts Into Practice
blocks.text: 4. Recap: The Why This Topic Puts Into Practice

blocks.content: The previous topic established six practical benefits driving cloud adoption, cost, agility, elasticity, speed, global reach, and focus, without yet addressing how an organization actually chooses among different ways of accessing those benefits.

Deployment models are precisely that how. Public cloud realizes all six benefits most fully. Private cloud trades some of those benefits for greater control. Hybrid cloud deliberately mixes both, exactly as demonstrated in this topic's bank example.

Understanding deployment models as the practical application of the previous topic's why, rather than as an unrelated new subject, is the correct way to connect this topic to everything already established earlier in this module.
The next topic gives each of these three models a full, direct, side by side comparison, building on both this topic's introduction and the previous topic's benefit framework together.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736026788-737946191.png
blocks.alt: Recap of why cloud, already covered above, applied in practice

blocks.content: 5. The Three Models at a Glance
blocks.text: 5. The Three Models at a Glance

blocks.content: Public cloud offers the fullest realization of the six benefits covered in the previous topic, at the cost of sharing underlying physical infrastructure with other customers, a tradeoff acceptable and even preferable for the overwhelming majority of workloads.

Private cloud offers the greatest control and the strongest isolation guarantees, at the cost of losing much of the elasticity, cost efficiency, and reduced operational burden that public cloud provides, since the organization still owns or exclusively leases the infrastructure.

Hybrid cloud offers a deliberate middle ground, letting an organization place each specific workload in whichever model best fits its specific requirements, at the cost of additional complexity in connecting and managing two distinct environments together.

This module's coverage of AWS specifically focuses primarily on the public cloud model, since that is what AWS itself directly provides, though hybrid architectures connecting to AWS are a genuinely common and well supported real world pattern.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736028557-640181645.png
blocks.alt: Public, private, and hybrid cloud models compared together

6. A Common Mistake: Choosing Before Understanding Needs
blocks.text: 6. A Common Mistake: Choosing Before Understanding Needs

blocks.content: A common mistake is selecting a deployment model, often defaulting reflexively to whichever model a previous employer used or whichever model is currently most discussed in industry conversation, before genuinely understanding the specific workload's own requirements.

A workload with no genuine regulatory or data residency requirement gains little from private cloud's additional cost and reduced elasticity, while a workload with a genuine, strict regulatory requirement may find public cloud alone insufficient regardless of its other benefits.

The correct approach, covered in more detail in the very next topic's decision framework, starts from the workload's actual requirements, compliance, control, cost sensitivity, and elasticity needs, and selects the deployment model that genuinely fits those requirements.

This mistake is particularly costly because migrating between deployment models after the fact, once significant infrastructure and application logic has been built around an initial, poorly considered choice, is considerably more expensive than choosing correctly from the start.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736030278-328125989.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of choosing a deployment model before understanding workload needs

blocks.content: 7. Deployment Models and This Course's Scope
blocks.text: 7. Deployment Models and This Course's Scope

blocks.content: This nineteen module course focuses overwhelmingly on AWS's public cloud services, since that is where the vast majority of real, hands on AWS engineering work actually happens, and it is where every remaining module's services and examples live.

Private and hybrid arrangements are mentioned where genuinely relevant, such as AWS Direct Connect and VPN connectivity covered in the Networking module, since these are the specific AWS services that make hybrid architectures like this topic's bank example possible.

Understanding that public cloud is this course's primary focus, while private and hybrid remain real, important patterns worth recognizing, sets accurate expectations for the specific, practical services covered across the remaining modules of this course.

This scope decision mirrors real world AWS engineering practice closely: most AWS engineers spend the overwhelming majority of their time working within the public cloud model, even at organizations that maintain some hybrid infrastructure elsewhere.
8. AWS Outposts: Public Cloud Hardware, On Premises
blocks.text: 8. AWS Outposts: Public Cloud Hardware, On Premises

blocks.content: AWS Outposts is a specific AWS offering worth knowing about at this introductory stage: physical racks of genuine AWS hardware, installed directly inside a customer's own on premises facility, running the same AWS services and APIs used in the public cloud.

This is a genuinely distinct pattern from the general public, private, and hybrid categories covered earlier in this topic, blurring the line between them by bringing AWS's own public cloud technology physically into a private, on premises location.

Outposts exists specifically for workloads with a genuine, low latency requirement to on premises systems, or a strict data residency requirement mandating physical presence in a specific facility, that neither pure public cloud nor a separate private cloud can satisfy.

This is an advanced, specialized pattern not covered in further depth in this introductory module, but recognizing it exists helps correctly interpret it if encountered later in this course or in real world AWS documentation.
9. Deployment Models and Organizational Change Management
blocks.text: 9. Deployment Models and Organizational Change Management

blocks.content: Adopting a new deployment model, particularly moving from private or hybrid toward greater public cloud reliance, is as much an organizational change management challenge as a technical one, often requiring new skills, new processes, and new ways of thinking about infrastructure.

Teams accustomed to owning and directly controlling physical hardware sometimes resist public cloud adoption not for a genuine technical reason, but from unfamiliarity or a perceived loss of control that the Shared Responsibility Model, covered later in this module, actually addresses directly.

Recognizing this human, organizational dimension alongside the purely technical decision framework covered earlier in this topic is genuinely useful for anyone involved in driving or supporting a real deployment model transition within their own organization.

This is not a technical detail this course covers in further depth, but it is worth naming explicitly here, since real world deployment model decisions are rarely purely technical exercises made in isolation from organizational context.
10. A Second Real Example: Media and Entertainment
blocks.text: 10. A Second Real Example: Media and Entertainment

blocks.content: Consider a media streaming company with wildly variable, unpredictable demand tied directly to content release schedules, where a single popular new release can cause traffic to spike by an order of magnitude within hours.

This kind of demand pattern is close to a worst case scenario for owned, private infrastructure, which would need to be sized for the largest plausible spike, leaving enormous amounts of capacity sitting idle during every ordinary, non spike period.

Public cloud, with its elasticity benefit covered in the Why Cloud topic, is an almost perfect fit for this specific demand pattern, letting the company scale dramatically for a release spike and scale back down immediately afterward.

This example, alongside the bank and healthcare examples already covered in this module, rounds out a genuinely broad picture of how different industries with different demand patterns and different regulatory contexts arrive at different, deliberate deployment model choices.
11. Checking a Workload's Deployment Model Fit Directly
blocks.text: 11. Checking a Workload's Deployment Model Fit Directly

blocks.content: A practical checklist for evaluating a specific workload's deployment model fit includes asking about regulatory requirements, existing infrastructure investment, demand predictability, and the genuine cost of any additional hybrid connectivity complexity.

Running through this checklist explicitly for any new, significant workload, rather than relying on organizational habit or the deployment model most recently used elsewhere, produces a more genuinely informed, defensible decision.

This checklist connects directly to the practical decision framework given full treatment in the very next topic, extending it slightly earlier here as a preview specifically for evaluating deployment model fit at the level of an individual workload.

Building this habit early in a career working with AWS pays off considerably, avoiding both the common mistake of defaulting to hybrid unnecessarily and the opposite mistake of forcing a genuinely regulated workload into public cloud without adequate justification.

["Ask about genuine regulatory or compliance requirements","Consider existing on premises infrastructure investment","Evaluate demand predictability and variability","Weigh the real cost of any additional hybrid connectivity complexity"]
items: Ask about genuine regulatory or compliance requirements
Consider existing on premises infrastructure investment
Weigh the real cost of any additional hybrid connectivity complexity

blocks.content: 12. How Deployment Model Choice Affects Later Modules
blocks.text: 12. How Deployment Model Choice Affects Later Modules

blocks.content: The deployment model choice made here has real, downstream consequences for nearly every later module in this course, particularly Networking in Module 6, where connecting public cloud resources to private infrastructure requires specific, deliberate configuration.

Security Services in Module 7 also differs meaningfully depending on deployment model, since a purely public cloud workload and a hybrid workload connecting back to on premises infrastructure have genuinely different security boundaries to consider and defend.

Recognizing this connection early helps frame why certain later modules devote specific attention to hybrid connectivity patterns, rather than assuming every AWS workload exists in complete isolation from any non AWS infrastructure.

For now, it is enough to understand that this early architectural decision, covered fully in the very next topic, ripples forward through many of the more advanced, practical topics covered later in this course.
13. Best Practices for Approaching Deployment Model Decisions
blocks.text: 13. Best Practices for Approaching Deployment Model Decisions

blocks.content: Start from the specific workload's actual requirements, compliance, data residency, control, and elasticity needs, rather than from organizational habit or industry trend, exactly as covered in this topic's common mistake section.

Recognize that deployment model decisions are rarely all or nothing for an entire organization. Different workloads within the same organization can, and often should, use different deployment models based on their own individual requirements.
Treat a deployment model choice as a genuine architectural decision with real migration cost if changed later, worth the deliberate, upfront evaluation the next topic's decision framework provides.

Default to public cloud unless a specific, genuine requirement points toward private or hybrid, reflecting both this course's primary focus and the reality that most workloads benefit most from public cloud's full realization of the previous topic's six benefits.

blocks.content: 14. The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

Cloud deployment models answer where infrastructure lives and who shares access to it, a genuinely distinct question from the service model question covered in a later topic in this module, and the choice carries real, lasting architectural consequences.

Public, private, and hybrid cloud each realize the six benefits from the previous topic to a different degree, and the right choice depends entirely on a specific workload's actual requirements, never on habit or industry trend alone.
The next topic gives all three models the full, direct, side by side comparison this introduction has been building toward, including a genuine, practical decision framework for choosing among them.

Keep this topic's bank example in mind. It is the clearest illustration in this module of why the right answer is often not one single model applied universally, but a deliberate mix matched to each workload's own specific needs.
This topic is now fully covered; Public vs Private vs Hybrid Cloud, giving each model the full comparison this overview promised, follows immediately next.
The where question this topic opened is now answered at the overview level, ready for the deeper comparison ahead.
Public cloud remains the correct default in nearly every case.
Hybrid architectures deserve deliberate justification, never reflexive adoption.
The right model fits the workload, not the other way around.

blocks.title: Cloud Deployment Models In Full
points: A cloud deployment model determines where infrastructure lives and who shares access to it, distinct from the service model question of how much of the stack you manage yourself.
Public cloud shares provider owned infrastructure across many customers; private cloud dedicates infrastructure entirely to one organization; hybrid cloud deliberately combines both.
The right deployment model depends on a specific workload's actual requirements, compliance, control, cost sensitivity, and elasticity, never on habit or industry trend.
Different workloads within the same organization can and often should use different deployment models, exactly as demonstrated in this topic's bank example.
Public vs Private vs Hybrid Cloud, covered next, gives all three models the full, direct comparison and practical decision framework this topic has been building toward.
